name: Raisin Black
lede: Raisin Black is a near-black with a faint purple cast, named for dried fruit and tracked across five different color systems since Werner's 1821 nomenclature.

sections.title: A black measured five ways
sections.body:
Werner's 1821 *Nomenclature of Colours*, the system Patrick Syme expanded from Abraham Werner's original, paired its blacks with natural analogs [1]. Werner's no. 22 gives the berry of deadly nightshade as a plant match for this one, and olivine ore as a mineral match, both read from an aged, scanned swatch, so the comparison is approximate [1]. Ridgway's 1912 atlas lists a near reading at plate XLIV, hue 65''', and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates its own record of the name to 1905, at plate 40 C 7 [1]. ISCC-NBS folded it into block 235 in 1955, calling it a purplish black, and RAL later gave it an approximate equivalent, RAL 8022 [1].

In Lab terms it sits at lightness 13, barely off true black, with a slight violet lean [1]. Its nearest library neighbors are [[dark-gunmetal|Dark gunmetal]] and [[eerie-black|Eerie Black]], both under five units away [1]. [[raisin-purple|Raisin Purple]] carries the same "Raisin" word toward a much lighter, visibly purple cousin [1]. A third library entry, [[vivid-black|Vivid black]], sits only slightly further out, among the handful of near-blacks this close together [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of it covers at least five percent of the canvas in 1,897 of our 23,781 archive paintings, as photographed, more common than 94 percent of our named colors [2]. It most often serves as a shadow, 56 percent of the 1,688 paintings our within-painting lens finds it in, and it peaks in the 1500s, in 173 of 2,231 paintings, at 1.3 times the expected rate [2]. Pieter van der Werff is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 19 of his 35 works here, 11.7 times his era's baseline [2]. The earliest dated painting is from 1201, 620 years before Werner's 1821 record, a floor set by thin early coverage, not a true first sighting; in printed English the phrase itself peaks in the 1920s [2].
